sections.h2: What is an Arizona beneficiary deed?
sections.html:
Arizona calls its transfer on death deed a beneficiary deed, and it passes real property to a named person when the owner dies. A.R.S. 33-405 says a deed that names a grantee beneficiary and expressly states it is effective on the owner's death transfers the interest at death, subject to every mortgage, lien and encumbrance the owner created or was subject to during life.

It names who receives the house at death. It does not change who owns the home today, and an owner who signs one remains free to sell, borrow against or live in the property.

sections.h2: How do you make an Arizona beneficiary deed valid?
sections.html:
It must be executed and recorded with the county recorder in the county where the house sits, before the owner dies. Subsection E of the statute makes recording before death a condition of validity, and a deed signed but left in a drawer does not work.

The statute also lays out what the deed can do:

  • Name several grantees, who can take as joint tenants with right of survivorship, tenants in common, community property, or another tenancy valid in Arizona.
  • Name a successor grantee beneficiary, with the condition that triggers the successor stated on the deed.
  • Convey to the trustee of a trust, even a revocable one.
  • Use the statutory form, which asks the owner to choose what happens if a beneficiary dies first: the gift becomes null and void, or becomes part of that beneficiary's estate.

If no named grantee survives the owner, the deed is void unless it says otherwise.

sections.h2: Can the owner change their mind or sell afterward?
sections.html:
Yes. The owner can revoke the deed at any time by recording a revocation before death, and no grantee has to sign or consent. Subsection I states that the signature, consent or notice to a grantee beneficiary is not required for any purpose during the owner's life.

Two more rules help a selling owner:

  • If more than one beneficiary deed is recorded for the same property, the last one recorded before death is the effective one (subsection G).
  • A later will does not revoke a recorded beneficiary deed (subsection J).

A sale made during life is one of the conveyances the beneficiary deed is subject to under subsection A. Whether a title company also wants a recorded revocation first is a question for that company.

sections.h2: Does a beneficiary deed clear mortgages and tax liens?
sections.html:
No. The transfer is subject to all conveyances, mortgages, deeds of trust, liens and other encumbrances. A beneficiary who receives the house receives the loan and any lien attached to it.

That has a practical effect on selling. A beneficiary who wants to sell must pay off a mortgage, unpaid property tax and other liens from the proceeds. If the house has a delinquent tax lien, the statutes covered on our Arizona tax lien and tax sale pages apply to the new owner just as they did to the old one.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a beneficiary deed in Arizona?
sections.html:
The statutory recording fee is $30 per instrument under A.R.S. 11-475, and Cochise County lists the same flat fee on its recorder page.

The affidavit of property value and its fee are normally appended to deeds. Section 11-1134(B)(12) exempts a transfer made under a beneficiary deed with only nominal actual consideration, and section 11-1133 requires the exemption to be noted on the face of the instrument at recording. The recorder refuses a deed that has neither a complete affidavit nor an exemption notation.

ItemWhat the statute says
Recording fee$30 per instrument (11-475)
Affidavit of property valueExempt for a nominal-consideration beneficiary deed (11-1134(B)(12))
Exemption noteMust appear on the face of the instrument (11-1134(C))
Recorded before deathRequired for validity (33-405(E))

sections.h2: How do joint owners and several beneficiaries change the picture?
sections.html:
Joint ownership changes who controls the outcome. When owners hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship or as community property with right of survivorship, a beneficiary deed signed by all surviving owners takes effect at the death of the last survivor (subsection D).

If fewer than all owners sign, the deed is valid only when the last surviving owner is one of the signers. If the last survivor did not sign, the transfer lapses and the deed is void. A surviving joint tenant or spouse keeps rights that prevail over the named grantee beneficiary.

With several beneficiaries, subsection B says that unless the deed provides otherwise, what each takes is that person's separate property and not community property. A house with three beneficiaries can therefore need three signatures at a sale, which affects how quickly a buyer can close.

sections.h2: What does the statutory form say?
sections.html:
The form in subsection K is short. It reads, in substance, that the owner conveys the described property to the grantee beneficiary effective on the owner's death, followed by the legal description and a choice about a beneficiary who dies first.

A separate revocation form appears in subsection L. It identifies the recorded deed by recording date and by docket, book, page or instrument number, and by county. The statute says a deed is sufficient if it complies with other applicable laws and substantially follows the form, so a recorder or title company will still look at the acknowledgment and the legal description.

sections.h2: What if the owner dies without a beneficiary deed?
sections.html:
Arizona offers affidavit routes for small estates, found in A.R.S. 14-3971. They help only when the numbers stay under the statutory limits.

For personal property, a successor can collect by affidavit 30 days after death when no personal representative is pending and the personal property, less liens, does not exceed $200,000.

For real property, a successor may file an affidavit of succession not sooner than six months after death. The real property in the estate, less liens, may not exceed $300,000, measured by the full cash value on the assessment rolls. The affidavit must state that funeral and last-illness expenses and all unsecured debts are paid, that the signers are entitled to the property by intestacy or a valid will, that no one else has a claim, and that no federal estate tax is due. A certified death certificate is attached, and the certified copy is recorded with the county recorder.

sections.h2: How does a beneficiary deed affect a cash sale after death?
sections.html:
The deed transfers the interest effective on the owner's death, so the beneficiary's title comes from the recorded deed. That title depends on the deed having been recorded before death and on no later revocation or later deed existing.

Before listing or signing a contract, a beneficiary should work through these questions with a title company or attorney:

  • Is the recorded deed the last one on file for this property, and was it recorded before the date of death?
  • Did any named beneficiary die first, and what does the deed say about that case?
  • What mortgage balance and unpaid taxes sit on the house today?
  • Are there several beneficiaries who must all sign the sale?

A buyer paying cash for an as-is house can take on repairs, clean-out and a tenant, which is a common situation for an inherited property.

faqs.q: What is a transfer on death deed called in Arizona?
faqs.a: It is called a beneficiary deed under A.R.S. 33-405. It transfers real property to a named grantee beneficiary when the owner dies.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to sign the deed?
faqs.a: No. The signature, consent or notice to the grantee beneficiary is not required during the owner's life.

faqs.q: When must the deed be recorded?
faqs.a: Before the owner's death, with the county recorder in the county where the property is located. Recording after death does not make a beneficiary deed valid.

faqs.q: Can I still sell my house if I recorded a beneficiary deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The deed takes effect only at death, so a living owner can sell, and can revoke the deed by recording a revocation.

faqs.q: Does a will cancel a beneficiary deed?
faqs.a: No. A beneficiary deed that is executed, acknowledged and recorded as the statute requires is not revoked by a later will.

faqs.q: What if only some of the joint owners sign?
faqs.a: The deed is valid only if the last surviving owner is one of the signers. If the last survivor did not sign, the transfer lapses and the deed is void.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary inherit the mortgage too?
faqs.a: Yes. The transfer is subject to mortgages, liens and encumbrances that existed when the owner died.
